title: Feature examples/status tables are outdated
description: FEATURE_EXAMPLES lists ReAct/Tool Registry as planned though they exist, and includes approval_step/agentorchestrator.approval which are not implemented. Examples import agentorchestrator.patterns which does not exist.
acceptance_criteria: - Update feature status table to reflect actual implementations\n- Remove or clearly mark aspirational examples\n- Fix imports to existing modules
notes: Updated FEATURE_EXAMPLES: marked ReAct/Tool Registry implemented with correct imports, replaced non-existent patterns/tool APIs, corrected event workflow example, removed/marked human-in-loop as planned, replaced aspirational deep research example with real examples, and aligned handoff/context-isolation/memory snippets with actual APIs.

title: Extras/deps missing for documented features
description: langchain_openai/langchain_anthropic are required by create_openai_summarizer/create_anthropic_summarizer but not in extras. watchdog is required for ao dev --watch but not in dev extras. aiohttp is used by connectors/agents but not declared. Docs mention agentorchestrator[openai] which doesn’t exist.
acceptance_criteria: - pyproject extras updated or docs adjusted\n- Dependencies reflect actual runtime needs\n- Quickstart/requirements updated accordingly
notes: Added missing extras (summarization alias, openai/anthropic, http/aiohttp) and watchdog in dev; expanded all/observability extras. Updated README and REQUIREMENTS for extras alignment and redis version; added dev docs note for watchdog.

title: Use LLMGatewayClassifier in decorator supervisor_chain
description: Simple decorator-based supervisor_chain still uses keyword routing. Add optional LLMGatewayClassifier when llm_client is provided (fallback to keyword for mock), pass history/rag_context/user_profile into classifier, and add a test/stub path.
notes: Simple decorator-based supervisor_chain still uses keyword routing; add optional LLMGatewayClassifier when llm_client is provided, keep keyword fallback for mock. Ensure history/rag_context are passed to classifier and add tests/stubs.

title: Add Redis-backed chat storage for decorator chains
description: Decorator-based flows lack persistent chat history. Implement ChatStorage backed by RedisService and allow AgentOrchestrator Context to read/write per-user/per-session/agent transcripts, mirroring Squad's InMemoryChatStorage. Wire into simple supervisor chain (pass history to classifier/agents) with config flag to enable. Provide small example/test stub.
notes: Added optional chat_storage to decorator supervisor_chain; defaults to InMemoryChatStorage, supports RedisChatStorage if provided. delegate_to_specialists now fetches per-agent history, passes it in context, and persists user/agent messages after responses.

title: resume_event_loop does not restore checkpoint context
description: AgentOrchestrator.resume_event_loop() loads RunCheckpoint but discards checkpoint.context_data and creates a fresh ChainContext. This loses state across resumes. In addition, run isolation still processes events with run_id=None.
acceptance_criteria:
- resume_event_loop restores context from checkpoint.context_data
- event loop resume preserves processed event history if needed
- run isolation behavior documented and tested
- Add unit/integration test for resume_event_loop

title: Resumable runs re-execute completed steps
description: ResumableChainRunner.resume()/retry_failed() re-run the full chain even when skip_completed=True, which can duplicate side effects and contradict resumability. This happens because DAGExecutor has no skip mechanism and resume only merges outputs into initial_data.
acceptance_criteria:
- DAGExecutor or ResumableChainRunner can skip completed steps
- resume() only executes pending/failed steps
- retry_failed() only executes failed steps
- Add unit test covering resume + side-effect step
- Docs/CLI mention actual behavior

title: Summarizer/Offload/TokenManager do not update context outputs
description: Summarizer/Offload/TokenManager modify StepResult.output but usually leave original large payloads in ChainContext unless keys match hardcoded patterns. Token counts may be under-reported and downstream steps see stale data.
acceptance_criteria: - Middleware updates context entries produced by a step (via produces/source_step)\n- Token counts reflect summarized/offloaded content\n- Add tests for context updates

title: CacheMiddleware cannot short-circuit step execution
description: CacheMiddleware sets _cache_hit/_cache_result flags but DAGExecutor never checks them, so steps still run. This defeats caching and can trigger side effects.
acceptance_criteria: - Cached results can bypass step execution in DAGExecutor\n- Cache hit returns output without executing handler\n- Add test covering cache short-circuit behavior

title: Docs contain broken imports and outdated API usage
description: Multiple docs reference non-existent modules (agentorchestrator.summarizers, agentorchestrator.services.RedisContextStore), use ao.* imports, and call ao.use_middleware even though public API is ao.use. Context store docs reference REDIS_URL and Mem0ContextStore(client=...) which are not supported.
acceptance_criteria: - All docs/examples use valid imports\n- ao.use_middleware references replaced with ao.use\n- Context store docs reflect actual API/signatures

title: Env var docs/doctor checks drift from config
description: Docs and CLI doctor reference env vars not used by config (LLM_BASE_URL, OTEL_ENABLED, LOG_FORMAT, AO_CACHE_*). Config uses LLM_SERVER_URL/LLM_GATEWAY_URL and AO_ENABLE_TRACING; .env.example includes SEC_AGENT_URL/NEWS_AGENT_URL while config expects AGENT_<NAME>_URL or AGENT_CONFIG.
acceptance_criteria: - Docs updated to match config env vars\n- CLI doctor checks aligned with supported env vars\n- .env.example reflects current configuration
notes: Aligned CLI observability with LOG_LEVEL/VERBOSE and updated scaffolding template env vars (LLM_MODEL_NAME, AO tracing, CHAIN_* and CACHE_TTL_SECONDS). Removed legacy AO_* logging/OTEL/LOG_FORMAT from template.

title: Multi-Agent Orchestrator System
description:
# Multi-Agent Orchestrator System

A comprehensive framework for managing multiple AI agents with intelligent routing, context management, and sophisticated team coordination.

## Goals
- Build a native SupervisorAgent with AgentOrchestrator that uses existing LLMGateway Client with OAuth
- Create flexible framework for managing multiple AI agents and handling complex conversations
- Implement robust memory and context management across agents
- Support YAML-based workflow definitions (future)
- Enable prompt optimization capabilities

## Technical Constraints
- Must work behind corporate proxy (cannot use Agent Squad package directly as it routes to Anthropic/OpenAI APIs)
- Must use existing LLMGateway Client with OAuth
- Pluggable interfaces for memory store, Redis, etc.

## Key Features Required
- Intelligent intent classification
- Parallel processing of agent queries
- Smart context management (Lead Agent Memory & Team Memory)
- Dynamic delegation to appropriate team members
- Support for streaming and non-streaming responses
- OpenTelemetry span tracing and application logs
- LLM as a judge and guardrails for all agents

## Priority Order
1. Core SupervisorAgent and Multi-Agent Orchestrator (foundational)
2. Memory & Context Management (required for coherent multi-agent conversations)
3. Prompt Optimization (quality improvement)
4. YAML-based Workflows (advanced feature, lower priority)

title: SupervisorAgent with Agents Coordination
description:
# SupervisorAgent with Agents Coordination

Implement a powerful SupervisorAgent that enables sophisticated team coordination between multiple specialized agents using an "agent-as-tools" architecture.

## Overview
A lead agent coordinates a team of specialized agents in parallel, maintaining context and delivering coherent responses.

## Core Features

### 1. Parallel Processing
- Execute multiple agent queries simultaneously
- Fan-out to multiple agents for concurrent processing
- Synchronization points for collecting results

### 2. Smart Context Management
- Maintain conversation history across all team members
- Agents have access to:
  - **Lead Agent Memory**: Supervisor's conversation history and decisions
  - **Team Memory**: Shared context across all team agents

### 3. Dynamic Delegation
- Intelligently distribute subtasks to appropriate team members
- Supervisor uses its own LLM to understand intent
- Decides which specialist agent is best suited for each task

## Integration Methods

### Method 1: Direct Usage
- Call directly for dedicated team coordination
- Best for linear chains (e.g., SEC + CapIQ + News)
- Connecting multiple agents in sequence

### Method 2: Classifier Integration
- Add as an agent within classifier
- Build complex hierarchical systems with multiple specialized teams
- Intelligent routing based on user queries

## Process Flow
```
Step 1: User asks a question
        "How do I optimize my Python code?"

Step 2: Supervisor analyzes
        - Reads the question
        - Uses its own LLM to understand intent
        - Decides which specialist agent is best suited

Step 3: Routes to specialist
        - Picks TechAgent (because it's about programming)
        - Forwards the question to TechAgent
        - TechAgent processes and responds

Step 4: Returns response
        - Supervisor receives TechAgent's response
        - Returns it to the user
```

## Built-in Classifier Behavior
The orchestrator has a built-in classifier that:
- Examines user input + chat history + agent descriptions
- Identifies the most appropriate agent
- Routes the request automatically

## Additional Requirements (from @sema)

### LLM & Embedding
- Custom LLM from LLM Gateway
- Custom embedding model from LLM Gateway

### RAG Integration
- RAG as a service integration with subagents
- Integrate via MCP connectors already available

### Dynamic Agent Creation
- Supervisor creates variable number of subagents based on request
- Allow customizations/configurations for different subagent types
- Pluggable interfaces (memory store, Redis, etc.)
  - Reference: https://rbcgithub.fg.rbc.com/rbc-cm/isa0-agent-arc/blob/feature/ao/agentorchestrator/services/redis.py

### Resource Management
- Dynamic resource allocation based on number of subagents needed

### Observability
- Application logs
- OpenTelemetry span tracing

### Quality & Safety
- LLM as a judge for all agents
- Guardrails for all agents
- Validation layer for agent outputs

### Skills
- Claude skills capability

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] SupervisorAgent can coordinate multiple specialist agents
- [ ] Parallel execution of agent queries works correctly
- [ ] Context is maintained across Lead Agent and Team Memory
- [ ] Dynamic delegation routes to appropriate agents
- [ ] Works with LLMGateway Client behind corporate proxy
- [ ] Configurable subagent types supported
- [ ] OpenTelemetry tracing implemented
- [ ] Guardrails and validation layer in place
notes: Added vector store service (memory/remote) and optional retrieve_context step in supervisor example; simple chain now passes rag_context/history to agents and enforces per-agent timeouts for safer delegation.

title: Multi-Agent Orchestrator Framework
description:
# Multi-Agent Orchestrator Framework

Flexible framework for managing multiple AI agents and handling complex conversations with intelligent query routing and context maintenance.

## Overview
The system offers pre-built components for quick deployment, while also allowing easy integration of custom agents and conversation message storage solutions.

## Architecture Flow
```
1. User Input
      ↓
2. Classifier Analysis
   - Leverages Agents' Characteristics
   - Leverages Agents' Conversation history
      ↓
3. Agent Selection
   - Select most appropriate agent for the task
      ↓
4. Agent Processing
   - Selected agent processes user input
      ↓
5. Conversation Storage
   - Orchestrator saves conversation
   - Updates Agents' Conversation history
      ↓
6. Response Delivery
   - Response returned to user
```

## Core Features

### 1. Intelligent Intent Classification
- Dynamically route queries to the most suitable agent based on context and content
- Examine user input + chat history + agent descriptions
- Identify the most appropriate agent
- Route the request automatically

### 2. Flexible Agent Responses
- Support for both streaming and non-streaming responses from different agents
- Async/await patterns for non-blocking operations
- Proper handling of long-running agent tasks

### 3. Context Management
- Maintain and utilize conversation context across multiple agents for coherent interactions
- Cross-agent context sharing
- Multi-turn conversation handling

### 4. Extensible Architecture
- Easily integrate new agents or customize existing ones
- Plugin-based agent registration
- Hot-swappable agent configurations

### 5. Pre-built Components
- A variety of ready-to-use agents
- Multiple classifier implementations available
- Template agents for common use cases

## Technical Constraints

### Why Not Agent Squad Package
Agent Squad package will NOT work in corporate environment because:
- Routes directly to Anthropic/OpenAI APIs for built-in classifier
- Even though open source, rerouting to LLM gateway requires forking and significant modifications

### Solution: Native Implementation
Build native SupervisorAgent with AgentOrchestrator that:
- Uses existing LLMGateway Client with OAuth
- Follows the same patterns as Agent Squad
- Works behind corporate proxy

## Key Differences from SupervisorAgent

| Aspect | SupervisorAgent | Orchestrator Framework |
|--------|-----------------|------------------------|
| Scope | One component | Entire system |
| Role | Specific agent type that delegates | Framework that manages all agents |
| Think of it as | The manager | The company infrastructure |

**Relationship**: SupervisorAgent runs *inside* the Orchestrator. The orchestrator is the foundation; the supervisor is one type of agent you can use within it.

## Implementation Requirements

### Agent Registry
- Register and discover agents dynamically
- Agent metadata (name, description, capabilities)
- Agent health monitoring

### Classifier System
- Pluggable classifier implementations
- Default classifier using LLMGateway
- Support for rule-based and ML-based classification

### Conversation Storage
- Pluggable storage backends
- Support for in-memory, Redis, and persistent storage
- Conversation history retrieval and management

### Response Handling
- Unified response format
- Streaming response support
- Error handling and fallbacks

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Agent registry with dynamic registration
- [ ] Classifier that routes queries to appropriate agents
- [ ] Conversation storage with pluggable backends
- [ ] Support for streaming and non-streaming responses
- [ ] Works with LLMGateway Client and OAuth
- [ ] Pre-built template agents available
- [ ] Extensible architecture for custom agents

title: Memory and Context Management
description:
# Memory & Context Management

Comprehensive memory and context management system for multi-agent orchestration, enabling coherent conversations across multiple agents and sessions.

## Memory Management Types

### 1. Short-term Memory
- **Purpose**: Conversation context within sessions
- **Scope**: Current session only
- **Storage**: In-memory or Redis
- **Use Cases**:
  - Current conversation turns
  - Active task state
  - Recent agent interactions

### 2. Long-term Memory
- **Purpose**: User preferences, historical interactions
- **Scope**: Across sessions
- **Storage**: Persistent database
- **Use Cases**:
  - User preferences and settings
  - Historical conversation summaries
  - Learned user patterns
  - Agent performance history

### 3. Working Memory
- **Purpose**: Task state, intermediate results
- **Scope**: Current task execution
- **Storage**: In-memory with optional persistence
- **Use Cases**:
  - Current task state and progress
  - Intermediate computation results
  - Agent coordination state
  - Pending sub-task queue

## Context Management Requirements

### 1. Context Window Optimization
- Monitor token usage across context window
- Implement efficient context packing
- Prioritize relevant context over old context

### 2. Smart Context Pruning and Summarization
- Implement summarization strategy for older conversation parts
- Prevent out-of-memory issues from context overflow
- Smart pruning without losing critical information
- Semantic compression of completed tasks

### 3. Multi-turn Conversation Handling
- Track conversation state across turns
- Handle interruptions and topic switches
- Maintain coherent narrative across agents

### 4. Cross-agent Context Sharing
- Share relevant context between agents
- Avoid redundant information retrieval
- Maintain consistency across agent responses

## Implementation Components

### Memory Store Interface
```python
class MemoryStore(Protocol):
    async def store(self, key: str, value: Any, ttl: Optional[int]) -> None: ...
    async def retrieve(self, key: str) -> Optional[Any]: ...
    async def delete(self, key: str) -> None: ...
    async def search(self, query: str, limit: int) -> List[Any]: ...
```

### Supported Backends
- **In-Memory**: Fast, ephemeral storage for development
- **Redis**: Distributed cache for production
- **PostgreSQL**: Persistent long-term storage
- **Vector Store**: Semantic search for context retrieval

### Context Manager
```python
class ContextManager:
    def get_context_window(self, max_tokens: int) -> Context: ...
    def add_message(self, message: Message) -> None: ...
    def prune_context(self, target_tokens: int) -> None: ...
    def summarize_history(self, messages: List[Message]) -> str: ...
```

## Key Challenges to Address

### 1. Session Management
- Track conversation history so each agent knows prior context
- Ensure session state is accessible across agent handoffs
- Handle session expiration and cleanup

### 2. Context Window Limits
- Implement summarization strategy for older conversation parts
- Prevent out-of-memory issues from context overflow
- Smart pruning without losing critical information

### 3. Cross-Agent Context
- Define what context each agent needs
- Avoid context pollution between unrelated agents
- Maintain privacy boundaries where needed

## Pluggable Interface Reference
Reference implementation: https://rbcgithub.fg.rbc.com/rbc-cm/isa0-agent-arc/blob/feature/ao/agentorchestrator/services/redis.py

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Short-term memory implementation with session scope
- [ ] Long-term memory with persistent storage
- [ ] Working memory for task state management
- [ ] Context window optimization with token monitoring
- [ ] Smart summarization and pruning
- [ ] Cross-agent context sharing mechanism
- [ ] Pluggable memory store interface
- [ ] Redis backend implementation
- [ ] Session management with proper cleanup

title: Generic YAML-based Entry Points for Workflows
description:
# Generic YAML-based Entry Points for Workflows

**Priority: Lower Priority**

Allow users to define AI agent workflows through either YAML configuration or a visual UI. The system translates both inputs into a standardized YAML format, constructs a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) at runtime, and executes the workflow with full observability and error handling.

## Core Concepts

### Dual Workflow Definition Methods

#### A. Direct YAML Authoring (Technical Users)
Users write workflow definitions in a standardized YAML schema:
- Version control integration (Git)
- Schema validation with immediate feedback
- Syntax highlighting and auto-completion in IDE
- Template library for common patterns
- Linting and best practices validation

#### B. UI-Based Configuration (Non-Technical Users)
Configure via interface → system generates YAML:
- Drag-and-drop visual workflow builder
- Node-based interface (similar to n8n, Dify, Windmill, Temporal)
- Real-time YAML preview as users configure
- Form-based node configuration
- Visual validation and error indicators
- Bidirectional sync: UI ↔ YAML

### Open-Source Workflow Builder Options to Evaluate

| Tool | Key Features |
|------|--------------|
| **n8n** | Self-hosted, extensive integrations, node-based |
| **Windmill** | Developer-first, scripts as workflows, TypeScript/Python support |
| **Prefect** | Python-native, data pipeline focus |
| **Temporal Workflow UI** | Durable execution, state management |
| **Argo Workflows** | Kubernetes-native, container orchestration |
| **Apache Airflow** | Mature, Python DAGs, extensive plugins |
| **Dagster** | Data-aware orchestration, asset-based |
| **Flyte** | ML/data workflows, type-safe |

**TODO**: Evaluate n8n or Windmill for fastest integration with customization capabilities.

### C. Unified Output
- Both approaches produce the same standardized YAML format
- YAML serves as the "source of truth"
- Users can switch between UI and YAML views seamlessly
- Version-controlled workflow definitions

## Dynamic DAG Construction

### Phase 1: YAML Parsing
1. Validate YAML syntax
2. Load workflow definition
3. Resolve variable references and expressions
4. Validate against schema

### Phase 2: DAG Building
1. Create node objects from agent definitions
2. Establish edges based on dependencies
3. Validate graph structure (no cycles, valid references)

### Phase 3: Optimization
1. **Topological sorting** for execution order
2. **Identify parallel execution opportunities** - nodes with no dependencies can run concurrently
3. **Calculate critical path** - longest path through DAG determines minimum execution time
4. **Optimize execution plan** - batch parallel operations, minimize wait times

## DAG Node Types

### 1. Agent Nodes
Execute AI agents/models:
- LLM inference calls
- RAG retrieval operations
- Fine-tuned model execution
- Multi-agent collaboration
- Skill invocation

### 2. Conditional Nodes
Branch based on conditions:
- Evaluate expressions
- Route to different paths
- Skip nodes based on logic
- Multi-way branching

### 3. Parallel Nodes
Execute multiple paths simultaneously:
- Fan-out to multiple agents
- Concurrent API calls
- Independent processing branches
- Synchronization points

## Context Propagation
- Each node has access to workflow context
- Outputs from previous nodes available via expression syntax like: nodes.node_id.outputs.field
- Shared memory for cross-node communication
- Workflow inputs accessible throughout execution

## Recovery Mechanisms

### Automatic Retry with Backoff
- Configurable retry attempts per node
- Exponential backoff strategy (1s, 2s, 4s, 8s...)
- Jitter to prevent thundering herd
- Retry on specific error types

### Error Handling
- Node-level error handlers
- Workflow-level fallback paths
- Dead-letter queue for failed executions
- Manual intervention triggers

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] YAML schema defined and documented
- [ ] YAML parser with validation
- [ ] DAG construction from YAML
- [ ] Topological sort and execution ordering
- [ ] Parallel execution support
- [ ] Conditional branching support
- [ ] Context propagation between nodes
- [ ] Retry mechanism with exponential backoff
- [ ] Error handling and recovery
- [ ] (Future) UI-based workflow builder integration

title: Prompt Optimization
description:
# Prompt Optimization

LLM-driven prompt optimization system that helps figure out the best prompt for given tasks.

## Overview
Implement a system where the LLM can analyze, evaluate, and optimize prompts to improve agent response quality and consistency.

## Goals
- Automatically optimize prompts for better agent performance
- Reduce prompt engineering burden on developers
- Improve consistency of agent responses
- Enable A/B testing of prompt variations

## Key Features

### 1. Prompt Analysis
- Analyze existing prompts for clarity and effectiveness
- Identify ambiguous or problematic prompt patterns
- Suggest improvements based on best practices

### 2. Prompt Generation
- Generate optimized prompts based on task descriptions
- Create prompt variations for testing
- Adapt prompts to different agent personalities/roles

### 3. Prompt Evaluation
- Measure prompt effectiveness using LLM-as-a-judge
- Compare prompt variations against baseline
- Track prompt performance metrics over time

### 4. Prompt Templates
- Library of optimized prompt templates
- Domain-specific prompt templates
- Easy customization and extension

## Implementation Components

### Prompt Optimizer
- Input: Task description + current prompt (optional)
- Output: Optimized prompt with explanation
- Method: Use LLM to analyze and improve prompts

### Prompt Evaluator
- Compare prompt outputs against expected results
- Score prompts on multiple dimensions:
  - Clarity
  - Specificity
  - Consistency
  - Task completion rate

### Prompt Registry
- Store and version prompts
- Track prompt performance history
- Enable prompt sharing across agents

## Integration Points
- Works with SupervisorAgent for team coordination prompts
- Integrates with Memory system for context-aware prompts
- Feeds into Guardrails for prompt safety validation

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Prompt analyzer identifies improvement opportunities
- [ ] Prompt optimizer generates improved versions
- [ ] Prompt evaluator scores prompt effectiveness
- [ ] Prompt registry stores and versions prompts
- [ ] LLM-as-a-judge integration for quality assessment
- [ ] A/B testing framework for prompt comparison

title: Cross-Cutting Concerns and Bottlenecks
description:
# Cross-Cutting Concerns and Bottlenecks

Key bottlenecks and concerns to address across the entire Multi-Agent Orchestrator system. These are critical issues that affect multiple components and must be considered throughout implementation.

## 1. Session Management

### Problem
Keep track of the conversation history so each agent knows what happened before.

### Requirements
- Track conversation history across agent handoffs
- Ensure session state is accessible to all agents
- Handle session creation, retrieval, and cleanup
- Support session persistence across service restarts

### Implementation Considerations
- Session ID generation and management
- Session storage backend (Redis, database)
- Session expiration and cleanup policies
- Session serialization format

---

## 2. Context Window Limits

### Problem
Make sure you have a plan to summarize older parts of the conversation so you don't run out of memory.

### Requirements
- Monitor token usage in context window
- Implement summarization for older conversation parts
- Prevent out-of-memory issues from context overflow
- Smart pruning without losing critical information

### Implementation Considerations
- Token counting for different LLM providers
- Summarization strategy selection
- Priority-based context retention
- Incremental summarization vs. batch

---

## 3. Coordination Between Agents

### Problem
Ensure that agents know when to step in and when to let another agent handle a query.

### Requirements
- Clear handoff protocols between agents
- Define when agents should step in vs. defer
- Avoid conflicts or duplicate responses
- Handle concurrent agent activations

### Implementation Considerations
- Agent capability matching
- Confidence thresholds for handoffs
- Conflict resolution strategies
- Agent priority and fallback chains

---

## 4. Response Consistency

### Problem
Keep the tone and quality of responses similar across different agents so users have a smooth experience.

### Requirements
- Maintain consistent tone across agents
- Ensure quality standards are met
- Unified response formatting
- Brand voice consistency

### Implementation Considerations
- Response post-processing layer
- Tone guidelines in system prompts
- Quality scoring and filtering
- Response template enforcement

---

## 5. Performance Overhead

### Problem
Make sure the system stays fast and doesn't slow down as more agents are added.

### Requirements
- System must stay fast as agents scale
- Monitor latency and resource usage
- Optimize parallel execution
- Minimize bottlenecks in routing

### Implementation Considerations
- Agent pool management
- Connection pooling for LLM calls
- Caching strategies (prompt cache, response cache)
- Load balancing across agent instances
- Async/non-blocking operations throughout

---

## Monitoring & Observability Requirements

### Metrics to Track
- Session creation/destruction rates
- Context window utilization per session
- Agent handoff frequency and success rate
- Response time per agent
- Error rates by agent type
- Memory usage trends

### Alerts to Configure
- Context window approaching limit
- Session count exceeding threshold
- Response latency spikes
- Agent failure rates
- Memory pressure warnings

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Session management implemented with proper lifecycle
- [ ] Context summarization strategy defined and implemented
- [ ] Agent coordination protocols documented and enforced
- [ ] Response consistency layer in place
- [ ] Performance benchmarks established
- [ ] Monitoring dashboards created
- [ ] Alert thresholds configured
